title: Stop Using RAG as Memory — Daniel Chalef, Zep

primary.label: Context Engineering & Memory
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 98%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is building domain-aware memory systems for AI agents using temporal knowledge graphs, which directly addresses context construction and durable conversational state. Zep is a cross-domain memory layer for AI agents and simultaneously a developer tool that software builders integrate into their systems. The presentation covers the design philosophy of domain-aware memory and demonstrates development practices including schema definition and agent tool construction. The content requires familiarity with programming languages, schema definition tools, and knowledge graph concepts, targeting intermediate practitioners. This is a conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair that includes a pre-recorded demo of a finance coach application built on Zep. Seven transcript-grounded evidence anchors directly support the classification, covering memory domain modeling, semantic similarity limitations, schema definition, ontology registration, and concurrent filtered search.

summary: Daniel Chalef contends there is no one-size-fits-all solution for AI agent memory and that memory should be modeled after the specific business domain. He criticizes vectorstore-based memory systems sold as memory for lacking relational and temporal awareness, leading agents astray with outdated or ambiguous information. He illustrates this with a media assistant example that incorrectly stores irrelevant facts (such as a dog named Melody or a 7 a.m. wake-up time) alongside relevant music preferences. Because retrieval relies on semantic similarity, querying for favorite tunes surfaces Melody due to superficial embedding proximity. Chalef emphasizes that semantic similarity is not business relevance and that simply dumping facts into a vector database makes it difficult to differentiate what should be returned. He presents Zep's solution using the open-source Graphiti temporal graph framework, which lets developers define custom entity types and edges with business rules on fields using Pydantic, Zod, or Go structs. A finance coach demo shows structured business objects—financial goals, debts, income sources—stored as a knowledge graph. Developers register these ontologies with Zep, and the system parses new messages to extract and populate the appropriate entities, demonstrated when a user mentions $5,000/month rent and Zep creates a debt account entity in the graph. Tools can run concurrent Zep searches filtered by specific node types for precise retrieval. Chalef references a paper describing how the system works.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction: No One-Size-Fits-All Memory
sections.summary: Chalef introduces the thesis that there is no one-size-fits-all memory and that memory should be modeled after the business domain, referencing his earlier talk on Graphiti's custom entities and edges.

sections.title: The Problem with Vector-Based Memory
sections.summary: Chalef explains that storing arbitrary facts in vector databases leads to irrelevant retrieval and hallucinations, using a media assistant example where a dog named Melody surfaces in a favorite tunes query. He emphasizes that semantic similarity is not business relevance and that domain-aware memory, not better semantic search, is needed.

sections.title: Demo: Finance Coach with Zep
sections.summary: Chalef demonstrates a finance coach application built on Zep, showing developer-defined business objects (financial goals, debts, income sources) defined via TypeScript schemas with field-level business rules. He shows ontology registration, live message parsing of $5,000/month rent into a debt account entity, and graph visualization of the user's knowledge graph.

sections.title: Closing: Paper Reference
sections.summary: Chalef references a paper describing how the system works, provides a link, and invites attendees to follow up with him afterward.
